claims.text: The as-synthesized FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles have uniform composition and size distribution.
Slower heating provides more time for surface atomic diffusion.
Surface atomic diffusion promotes formation of a premelted liquid-like surface layer.
Formation of a premelted liquid-like surface layer lowers the effective melting-onset temperature.
Rapid heating inhibits surface diffusion and associated surface segregation or premelting.
Suppression of premelting under rapid heating causes a more abrupt phase transition.
Under rapid heating, the abrupt transition occurs when the bulk melting temperature is reached.
Nanoparticles heated at 5 °C/min will begin melting at a lower temperature than nanoparticles heated at 50 °C/min.
Nanoparticles heated at 5 °C/min will exhibit a more gradual melting transition than nanoparticles heated at 50 °C/min.
Slow heating will produce a gradually emerging liquid-like surface layer observable by TEM.
Rapid heating will produce minimal premelting features before the main transition.
A 20 °C/min heating rate will yield transition behavior intermediate between that at 5 °C/min and 50 °C/min.
The baseline nanoparticles exhibit no premelting at or near their baseline melting point under conventional heating protocols.
Reactive gases or uncontrolled temperature gradients may confound surface-diffusion dynamics.
Heating-rate control of surface diffusion is well supported in nanoscale systems generally.
